title: Oil at the threshold
hookLine: in the house where praise is sung, friends pour oil at the door for the bride, whose day has come (Gauri Deepaki M1, ang 12)
last: JAI GHAR KEERAT — IN THE HOUSE OF PRAISE.

lines: THE DATE IS FIXED AND WRITTEN.
cards: A Punjabi wedding doesn't start on the wedding day. It starts weeks before, with a date. Someone fixes the auspicious day, it's written down, letters go out.
Then the house fills: cousins, aunties, songs every evening, turmeric, too much food.
And at the doorway, a small custom some families still keep: when the bride or groom arrives, a woman of the house pours a little oil on either side of the door, as welcome and blessing.
Guru Nanak puts that whole scene at the end of the night song's first hymn.

teach.b: The last verses sound like a wedding invitation. In paraphrase: the year and the moment have been written; come, friends, together, pour the oil. Give me your blessings, friends, so that I may meet my Lord.
The word for that fixed date is saahaa, the wedding day set in advance.
In Gurbani the soul is often pictured as a bride, and God as the beloved she longs to meet. So the bride is the soul, and the wedding is the meeting with the One. Then the hymn turns, gently.

teach.h: A CALL TO EVERY HOUSE, EVERY DAY.
teach.b: In paraphrase: into every house this message is sent; these calls come every day. Remember the One who sends the call, says Nanak; those days are drawing near.

Commentators read the wedding here as death, the soul's day to go and meet the Beloved. Read that way, the verse belongs in a night song, and every night becomes a small rehearsal of letting go. But the mood isn't dread.

teach.h: FRIENDS AT THE DOOR WITH BLESSINGS.
teach.b: The friends aren't weeping at the door; they're pouring oil and giving blessings. And the summons isn't sent to one unlucky house.
It goes to every house, every day. Nobody is singled out; nobody is skipped. The hymn doesn't ask you to fear the letter.
It asks you to be the kind of house where praise is sung when it arrives, with friends at the door when it's your turn.

how: Sikhs recite these verses every night as the close of Kirtan Sohila's first hymn, and Kirtan Sohila is also recited at a Sikh cremation; some Punjabi families still keep the custom of pouring oil at the threshold when a bride or groom arrives.

o: the wedding date, fixed and written in advance
the song friends sing at the bride's farewell
a dowry gift sent with the bride to her new home

games.q: the wedding in the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: the wedding date, fixed in advance

s: in the hymn, the summons goes to one unlucky house
it goes into every house, and the calls come every day.
Gurbani often pictures the soul as a bride
and God as the beloved she longs to meet.
the friends at the door are weeping
they pour oil and give blessings, as at a wedding.

games.q: the wedding date has been written, and the bride's day is near. what do her friends do?
o: shut the door and hope the day passes.
pour oil at the threshold and give their blessings.
argue about whether the date is right.
games.why: the hymn asks the friends to come together, pour the oil and bless her, so she may meet her Lord.

practice: Picture a door you know well, a parent's front door, a friend's apartment, your own, and see the handle, the step, the light.
Stand there like one of the friends in the hymn and wish whoever lives inside well: may this house be well. If you pray, say Waheguru softly for the people behind it.

wordCard.voice: Saahaa, the fixed wedding date: the wedding welcome Guru Nanak places at the end of Sohila's first hymn, where friends bless the bride, the soul, whose day has been written.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: saahaa, the fixed wedding date; in the hymn, the day the soul is called.

carryVoice: Your line: the bride is called. The call comes to every house, and friends come with blessings. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Gauri Deepaki M1, Ang 12 (Kirtan Sohila, hymn 1, closing verses)
